clue.text: Insight in caper cut by Frenchman

indicators.note: in tells us the answer sits inside the run of letters of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A Frenchman edits a madcap escapade and finds some insight in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' points inside 'caper cut': drop the outer C and T. 'by Frenchman' hints that the word is borrowed from French.
explanation.definitionFit: A French loanword for a brief, illuminating perception or summary.

clue.text: Foot of a peasant fractured

indicators.note: something fractured is broken into pieces, so the letters before it are reassembled

explanation.surface: A peasant's foot is broken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foot' looks anatomical; it is a metrical foot in verse.
explanation.definitionFit: A metrical unit of two short syllables and one long.

clue.text: Expatiate on effect of Alice's cake

explanation.surface: Talking at length about what Alice's cake did.
explanation.walkthrough: In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland a cake marked 'Eat me' makes Alice grow huge.
explanation.definitionFit: To enlarge on a topic is to speak at length; the cake made Alice grow bigger.

clue.text: Low-temperature treatment of revenant by Dennis Potter Barstow's dimwit produces Brian O'Nolan masterwork (2,4-3-5)

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held merges two clues: 'Low-temperature treatment of revenant by Dennis Potter' runs straight into 5-down's 'Barstow's dimwit produces Brian O'Nolan masterwork (2,4-3-5)', so the text is shown on two lights

clue.text: Later echo (we hear) of leading Middlemarch character

definitions.text: Later echo (we hear) of leading Middlemarch character

parts.words: Later echo (we hear) of leading Middlemarch character
parts.note: George Eliot's dry scholar in Middlemarch shares his name with the real Renaissance classical scholar Isaac, so the fictional man is a later echo of that name

explanation.surface: A literary critic notes that a Middlemarch figure recalls someone earlier.
explanation.walkthrough: The novel's pedant echoes Isaac of the same surname, a Huguenot classical scholar of the 1600s.
explanation.definitionFit: The dusty pedant whom Dorothea marries in George Eliot's novel.

clue.text: Barstow's dimwit produces Brian O'Nolan masterwork

indicators.note: produces means the letters before it are made into something new

parts.note: the possessive S counts as a letter here

explanation.surface: A dim character by novelist Stan Barstow writes an Irish classic.
explanation.walkthrough: Brian O'Nolan wrote as Flann O'Brien; Stan Barstow was an English novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: Flann O'Brien's (Brian O'Nolan's) 1939 metafictional first novel.

clue.text: "England's on the — hear the hammers ring -" (Kipling)

definitions.text: "England's on the — hear the hammers ring -" (Kipling)

parts.words: "England's on the — hear the hammers ring -" (Kipling)
parts.note: fill the gap in Kipling's line with the smith's block that hammers ring on

explanation.surface: A gapped quotation from a Kipling poem.
explanation.definitionFit: The iron block a blacksmith hammers metal on, the word missing from the line.

clue.text: Units of energy in good French exponent of élan vital

indicators.note: in places the energy units inside the French word

parts.note: bon is French for good
ergs are units of energy

explanation.surface: Energy units inside a good French philosopher of the life force.
explanation.walkthrough: Henri Bergson coined élan vital, the vital impetus.
explanation.definitionFit: The French philosopher who proposed a vital impetus driving evolution.

clue.text: Squeamish reaction by Sartre

parts.note: a feeling of sickness, and also the title of Sartre's first novel

explanation.surface: Sartre feels queasy.
explanation.definitionFit: A feeling of sickness; La Nausée is Sartre's 1938 novel.

clue.text: Advice from the Fortunate Isles, such as "Gather ye rosebuds while ye may"

definitions.text: Advice from the Fortunate Isles, such as "Gather ye rosebuds while ye may"

parts.words: Advice from the Fortunate Isles, such as "Gather ye rosebuds while ye may"
parts.note: the Fortunate Isles are the Hesperides, the title of Herrick's collection containing his poem urging virgins to make much of time

explanation.surface: Advice from a paradise, telling young people to seize the day.
explanation.walkthrough: Herrick's poem 'To the Virgins, to Make Much of Time' appears in his Hesperides, named after the Fortunate Isles.
explanation.definitionFit: Herrick's poem is guidance addressed to young women.

clue.text: Arthur Miller's theatrical progeny

parts.note: read straight, the playwright's children; read as a title, one of his plays, whose name is a phrase about a father's offspring

explanation.surface: A remark about the children of the American playwright.
explanation.definitionFit: Title of Miller's 1947 play, which also reads as a phrase meaning every one of the speaker's male children.

clue.text: Contents of The Old Curiosity Shop

definitions.text: Contents of The Old Curiosity Shop

parts.words: Contents of The Old Curiosity Shop
parts.note: Dickens's title names a shop of curios; its stock would be objets d'art and bric-a-brac

explanation.surface: An inventory of what Dickens's shop held.
explanation.definitionFit: A collective term for curios and fine art objects, exactly what a curiosity shop sells.

clue.text: Suitor misled by The Silver Box?

definitions.text: Suitor misled by The Silver Box?

parts.words: Suitor misled by The Silver Box?
parts.note: in The Merchant of Venice one of Portia's suitors wrongly chooses the silver casket; The Silver Box is also a Galsworthy play title, adding the misleading literary gloss

explanation.surface: A suitor is fooled by a play by Galsworthy.
explanation.walkthrough: The Silver Box looks like the Galsworthy play, but it is the silver casket Portia's suitor picks in Shakespeare.
explanation.definitionFit: The Prince in Shakespeare's Venetian comedy who picks the silver casket and loses Portia.

clue.text: Diesel's to be overhauled (not working)

indicators.note: an engine to be overhauled is taken apart and rebuilt, so the letters before it are rearranged

parts.note: the possessive S counts here as a letter of the fodder

explanation.surface: A diesel engine is due for an overhaul and so out of action.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic, poetic word for idleness, the state of doing nothing.

clue.text: An experiment writer is a mug

explanation.surface: An experimental author is called a fool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mug' looks like an insult for the writer; it is a beer tankard.
explanation.definitionFit: Gertrude of that surname wrote experimental modernist prose; the same word is a German beer tankard.

clue.text: When did the old seaman drop a hand?

definitions.text: When did the old seaman drop a hand?

parts.words: When did the old seaman drop a hand?
parts.note: in Coleridge's Ancient Mariner, the mariner releases the wedding guest, and the poem uses an archaic word for 'soon after' at that moment

explanation.surface: A question about when a sailor lost his grip.
explanation.walkthrough: The line in Coleridge's poem runs 'Eftsoons his hand dropt he', the old seaman being the Ancient Mariner.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic adverb meaning soon afterwards, the word Coleridge used for that moment.

clue.text: A contribution by "M. A. Titmarsh" to Christmas Books

definitions.text: A contribution by "M. A. Titmarsh" to Christmas Books

parts.words: A contribution by "M. A. Titmarsh" to Christmas Books
parts.note: Titmarsh was Thackeray's pen name, and one of his Christmas Books is a sketch of a neighbourhood road

explanation.surface: A piece by a pseudonymous author in a festive collection.
explanation.walkthrough: Michael Angelo Titmarsh was a pen name of Thackeray.
explanation.definitionFit: Thackeray's 1848 Christmas Book sketching the residents of a London road.

clue.text: Fielding characters in Zane Grey oeuvre

explanation.surface: Characters of Henry Fielding appear in cowboy novels.
explanation.walkthrough: Squire Western and his daughter Sophia are in Fielding's Tom Jones; Zane Grey wrote cowboy novels.
explanation.definitionFit: Squire Western and Sophia of Tom Jones; also cowboy stories set in the American frontier.

clue.text: Puzzle out crime for victim of Verona vendetta

indicators.note: to puzzle out something is to work it out, so the letters that follow must be worked into a new order

explanation.surface: Detectives solving a murder in a Verona feud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Puzzle out' reads as a phrasal verb, but 'out' is part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Romeo's friend in Shakespeare's play, killed by Tybalt in the Montague-Capulet feud.

clue.text: Partly revel in a work much admired by Jane Austen

definitions.text: work much admired by Jane Austen

indicators.note: Partly says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Delighting in a novel that Jane Austen admired.
explanation.definitionFit: Fanny Burney's 1778 epistolary novel, which Austen praised.

clue.text: Historian of The Black Arrow setting

indicators.note: of here means drawn out of, so the name is taken from within the letters of the words that follow

explanation.surface: Asking which scholar wrote about the period in which Stevenson set his novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites thinking about the Wars of the Roses, the novel's period; instead the name runs across the end of 'Arrow' and the start of 'setting'.
explanation.definitionFit: A. L. Rowse was a prolific Oxford scholar of Tudor England.

clue.text: Wodehouse swore to revise his hero's name

indicators.note: to revise text is to rework it, so the letters before are rearranged

explanation.surface: P. G. Wodehouse vows to change his protagonist's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Bertie, the hapless gentleman narrator of Wodehouse's Jeeves stories.

clue.text: Writer mentioned in Christabel (locally revered)

indicators.note: mentioned in says the name is spoken within the words that follow, sitting inside them

explanation.surface: An author is named in Coleridge's poem, which is honoured locally.
explanation.walkthrough: Christabel looks like the Coleridge poem; its letters end with the writer's first half.
explanation.definitionFit: Hilaire Belloc, the Anglo-French author of Cautionary Tales.

clue.text: Smoothing over, rather late in the day

explanation.surface: Someone tidies up a problem, though somewhat belatedly.
explanation.definitionFit: Levelling or making flat; also the close of the day, after afternoon.

clue.text: Rebellious tribe, very cold, and supported by Northern ireland

indicators.note: in a down answer, a piece supported by another sits on top of it

parts.note: ice is very cold

explanation.surface: A rebel tribe freezing, propped up by Northern Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: The Iceni were Boudicca's tribe, who rose against Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient British tribe led by Boudicca in revolt against Roman rule.

clue.text: Anthem made by brass ensemble, or tin trio?

indicators.note: brass instruments formed into an ensemble suggests the metal letters being regrouped into a new order

explanation.surface: A church anthem played by brass, or perhaps by three tinny players.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that a 'tin trio' is a brass ensemble of sorts, signalling its letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The psalm or antiphon sung as the priest approaches the altar at the start of Mass.

clue.text: French law concerning flower

parts.note: loi is French for law
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: A French statute about a blossom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flower' is crossword shorthand for a river, something that flows.
explanation.definitionFit: A river is something that flows, and this is France's longest river.

clue.text: Sort of special day Hawthorne had in mind?

definitions.text: Sort of special day Hawthorne had in mind?

parts.words: Sort of special day Hawthorne had in mind?
parts.note: a memorable occasion is marked on the calendar in a colour, and Hawthorne wrote The Scarlet Letter

explanation.surface: Wondering which notable date the American novelist was thinking of.
explanation.definitionFit: Describes a memorable day, from saints' days printed in colour in old calendars.

clue.text: "The affair is over, lives" wrote Lovelace

definitions.text: "The affair is over, lives" wrote Lovelace

parts.words: "The affair is over, lives" wrote Lovelace
parts.note: in Richardson's novel the rake Lovelace writes a famous letter announcing the affair is over and naming the heroine who still lives

explanation.surface: A line from a cavalier's letter about the end of an affair.
explanation.walkthrough: Lovelace suggests the poet Richard Lovelace, but he is the rake of Richardson's epistolary novel, who wrote 'And now, Belford, I can go no farther. The affair is over. Clarissa lives.'
explanation.definitionFit: The heroine of Samuel Richardson's novel, the name missing from Lovelace's letter.

clue.text: Typhoon, and The Tempest, eg

parts.note: Conrad's Typhoon and Shakespeare's Tempest are both literary titles naming violent weather

explanation.surface: Examples of fierce weather, or of works named after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Violent disturbances of the atmosphere, which both titles name.
